---
title: "UFW Basics: Uncomplicated Firewall"
---

`ufw` (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a friendly command-line front-end for Linux's packet filter. Ubuntu ships it by default, and it is available on Debian and most derivatives. It doesn't filter packets itself. It turns simple commands like `ufw allow 22/tcp` into the much more verbose `iptables`/`nftables` rules that the kernel's **netfilter** subsystem enforces.

```
  You                     Translator                 Kernel (does the real work)
 ──────                  ────────────               ─────────────────────────────
 ufw allow 443/tcp  ──►   ufw  ──►  iptables / nftables rules  ──►  netfilter
                          │                                           │
                          └─ stores rules in /etc/ufw/                └─ inspects every
                             (user.rules, before.rules...)               packet in/out
```

macOS doesn't have `ufw`, since it uses `pf`. To practice, spin up an Ubuntu VM with OrbStack, UTM, or Multipass (`brew install multipass`, then `multipass launch --name fw-lab`). That gives you a disposable machine where locking yourself out costs nothing.

---

## 1. The mental model: policies + rules

Each packet is checked against your rules **top to bottom**, and the **first matching rule wins**. If nothing matches, the **default policy** decides.

```
 Incoming packet (e.g., TCP to port 443 from 10.1.2.3)
        │
        ▼
 ┌──────────────────────┐   match?  ──yes──►  ALLOW / DENY / REJECT / LIMIT
 │ Rule 1               │
 └──────────┬───────────┘
            │ no
            ▼
 ┌──────────────────────┐   match?  ──yes──►  action
 │ Rule 2               │
 └──────────┬───────────┘
            │ no
            ▼
          ...
            │ nothing matched
            ▼
 ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ DEFAULT POLICY       │  (usually: deny incoming, allow outgoing)
 └──────────────────────┘
```

The sensible baseline for almost every server is **deny all incoming, allow all outgoing**, then open only what you need:

```bash
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
```

---

## 2. Enabling it safely (don't lock yourself out!)

This is the #1 beginner mistake. If you're connected over SSH and enable ufw with a deny-incoming policy, your session gets cut off. **Always allow SSH first:**

```bash
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH        # or: sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw enable               # now safe
sudo ufw status verbose
```

Example output:

```
Status: active
Logging: on (low)
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), disabled (routed)

To                         Action      From
--                         ------      ----
22/tcp (OpenSSH)           ALLOW IN    Anywhere
22/tcp (OpenSSH (v6))      ALLOW IN    Anywhere (v6)
```

ufw handles IPv4 and IPv6 together as long as `IPV6=yes` is set in `/etc/default/ufw`, which is the default. That's why each rule appears twice.

---

## 3. Core commands cheat sheet

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| Check status | `sudo ufw status` / `status verbose` / `status numbered` |
| Turn on / off | `sudo ufw enable` / `sudo ufw disable` |
| Allow a port | `sudo ufw allow 80/tcp` |
| Allow a port range | `sudo ufw allow 6000:6007/tcp` |
| Allow from one IP | `sudo ufw allow from 203.0.113.5` |
| Allow a subnet to a port | `sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 22 proto tcp` |
| Deny a port | `sudo ufw deny 3306` |
| Rate-limit (anti brute-force) | `sudo ufw limit 22/tcp` |
| Delete by rule | `sudo ufw delete allow 80/tcp` |
| Delete by number | `sudo ufw status numbered`, then `sudo ufw delete 3` |
| Insert at a position | `sudo ufw insert 1 deny from 198.51.100.7` |
| Allow on one interface | `sudo ufw allow in on eth1 to any port 5432` |
| Logging | `sudo ufw logging on` (logs in `/var/log/ufw.log`) |
| Wipe everything | `sudo ufw reset` |
| Test without applying | add `--dry-run`, e.g. `sudo ufw --dry-run allow 80` |

### The full rule grammar

Most commands are shorthand for this general form:

```
ufw [insert N] ACTION [in|out] [on IFACE] [proto PROTO]
    from SRC [port SPORT]  to DST [port DPORT]

 ACTION = allow | deny | reject | limit
```

---

## 4. `deny` vs `reject` vs `limit`

```
 deny    ──►  silently drop the packet
              client waits... and times out (stealthy, slower for attacker)

 reject  ──►  drop + send back "connection refused" (ICMP/TCP RST)
              client fails fast (friendlier on internal networks)

 limit   ──►  allow, BUT block an IP that opens ≥ 6 connections in 30 sec
              great for SSH brute-force protection
```

---

## 5. Order matters: a classic trap

Say you want to block one bad IP, but you already allowed SSH for everyone:

```bash
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw deny from 198.51.100.7     # appended as rule #2
```

```
 [1] ALLOW 22/tcp from Anywhere        ◄── 198.51.100.7 matches HERE first → allowed!
 [2] DENY  from 198.51.100.7           ◄── never reached for SSH traffic
```

The fix is to **insert** the deny rule above the allow:

```bash
sudo ufw insert 1 deny from 198.51.100.7
```

---

## 6. Application profiles

Packages can register named profiles in `/etc/ufw/applications.d/`, so you don't have to remember port numbers:

```bash
sudo ufw app list                    # e.g. OpenSSH, Nginx Full, Nginx HTTP, Nginx HTTPS
sudo ufw app info "Nginx Full"       # shows ports 80,443/tcp
sudo ufw allow "Nginx Full"
```

---

## 7. A realistic example: a web app server on a hospital network

Scenario: a server hosts a web app over HTTPS for everyone. SSH should come only from an internal admin subnet, and PostgreSQL only from the app server.

```
            Internet / hospital users
                     │  443
                     ▼
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  Server (ufw)                              │
 │   443/tcp  ← anyone                        │
 │    22/tcp  ← 10.10.0.0/16 only (limited)   │
 │  5432/tcp  ← 10.10.5.20 only               │
 │  everything else ← DENIED                  │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```bash
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing

sudo ufw limit from 10.10.0.0/16 to any port 22 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw allow from 10.10.5.20 to any port 5432 proto tcp

sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status numbered
```

---

## 8. Important gotcha: Docker bypasses ufw

This one matters for R&D teams deploying containers. When you publish a port with `docker run -p 8080:80`, Docker writes its own iptables rules. Those rules are evaluated **before** ufw's rules, so the port can be reachable from outside **even though `ufw status` doesn't show it as allowed**.

```
 packet ──► Docker's DOCKER-USER / FORWARD chain ──► container   (ufw never consulted!)
        └─► ufw chains (INPUT) ──► host services
```

There are a few common mitigations:

* **Bind to localhost** and put a reverse proxy in front: `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`.
* **Add rules to the `DOCKER-USER` chain** yourself.
* **Use a helper** such as the community `ufw-docker` project.

---

## 9. Where things live

```
/etc/default/ufw               # global settings (IPV6=yes, default forward policy)
/etc/ufw/user.rules            # rules you add via `ufw allow...` (IPv4)
/etc/ufw/user6.rules           # same, IPv6
/etc/ufw/before.rules          # rules applied before yours (e.g., ICMP ping, NAT)
/etc/ufw/applications.d/       # app profiles
/var/log/ufw.log               # log output (when logging is on)
```

---

## Try it yourself (in a VM)

1. Set the default policies, allow SSH, and enable ufw.
2. Install nginx (`sudo apt install nginx`) and allow only `"Nginx HTTP"`.
3. From your Mac, run `curl http://<vm-ip>`. It should work.
4. Run `sudo ufw delete allow "Nginx HTTP"` and curl again. It should now hang, because the packet is being dropped.
5. Change the rule to `reject` instead of removing it, and notice how curl now fails instantly instead of timing out.
